children.title: Purified lips and a humble remnant
Song of joy: the LORD in your midst

bigStory: Zephaniah gathers the prophetic theme of the Day of the LORD into a single sweeping vision of judgment followed by a joyful restored people. Its description of that day as a 'day of wrath' (Zeph 1:15) inspired the medieval hymn *Dies Irae*, and its picture of the LORD as king in Zion's midst anticipates the gospel's announcement of God dwelling with his people.
canonNote: Ninth book of the Twelve and the last of the pre-exilic prophets in its order; Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi follow from the post-exilic period.

name: Haggai
genre: Prophecy (dated prophetic sermons with brief narrative)

authorship.traditional: Haggai the prophet, active with Zechariah in encouraging the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14).
authorship.scholarly: The messages are widely accepted as Haggai's, but they are reported in the third person, so many scholars think a close associate or editor arranged them soon afterward, perhaps together with Zech 1-8 as a combined work on the temple's rebuilding.

audience: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest and the returned exiles in Jerusalem, who had let the temple lie in ruins while building their own houses.
setting: Jerusalem in the second year of Darius I of Persia, between August and December 520 BC, about eighteen years after the first return.
purpose: To rouse the community to rebuild the temple, to explain their economic hardship as the result of misplaced priorities, and to promise that God's glory would fill the house and that Zerubbabel would be his chosen signet ring.
themes: Consider your ways: priorities and God's house
The latter glory greater than the former

outline.title: Call to rebuild and the people's response
The glory of the latter house
From this day I will bless you

bigStory: Haggai marks the rebuilding of the second temple and keeps alive the hope attached to David's line through Zerubbabel, who appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:12-13). Hebrews quotes Hag 2:6 about God shaking heaven and earth to point to an unshakable kingdom (Heb 12:26-28).
canonNote: Tenth book of the Twelve; along with Zechariah and Malachi it belongs to the post-exilic prophets.

name: Zechariah
genre: Prophecy (night visions, sermons and apocalyptic-style oracles)

authorship.traditional: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (Zech 1:1), a priest-prophet who returned from exile and worked alongside Haggai (Ezra 5:1). Defenders of unity point to shared themes across the book, such as the cleansing of Jerusalem, the shepherd and the coming king.
authorship.scholarly: Most scholars distinguish Zech 1-8 (dated to 520–518 BC, from Zechariah himself) from Zech 9-14 (often called Deutero-Zechariah, with no dates, a different style and a looser historical setting), which many place in the 5th century or later, perhaps the early Greek period given the mention of Greece (Zech 9:13). Some further divide Zech 9-11 and Zech 12-14, each introduced by 'the burden of the word of the LORD'.

audience: The returned exiles in Jerusalem and their leaders Zerubbabel and Joshua, discouraged by small beginnings and foreign domination.
setting: Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the temple under Darius I (from 520 BC), with later oracles looking toward future conflicts and the final day of the LORD.
purpose: To call the people to return to the LORD, to encourage temple rebuilding through visions of God's renewed care for Jerusalem, and to announce a coming humble king, a rejected shepherd and the final day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.
themes: Return to me and I will return to you
Not by might, but by my Spirit
Cleansing of the priesthood and the land
The pierced one and the struck shepherd
The LORD king over all the earth

children.title: Flying scroll, woman in a basket, four chariots

outline.title: Questions about fasting; promises to Zion
First burden: the coming king and the shepherds

children.title: Your king comes on a donkey
The rejected shepherd and thirty pieces of silver

outline.title: Second burden: the day of the LORD

children.title: A fountain for cleansing; the shepherd struck
The LORD king over all the earth

bigStory: Zechariah keeps the hope of a coming king and a cleansed people alive in the modest days after the exile. The Gospels draw on it heavily in the passion story: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey (Matt 21:4-5), is betrayed for thirty pieces of silver (Matt 27:9-10), is the struck shepherd whose sheep scatter (Matt 26:31) and the pierced one on whom people look (John 19:37).
canonNote: Eleventh book of the Twelve and the longest of them. Matt 27:9-10 attributes a passage drawing on Zech 11:12-13 to Jeremiah, probably because it combines Zechariah with themes from Jeremiah (e.g. Jer 32:6-9).

name: Malachi
genre: Prophecy (disputation speeches)

authorship.traditional: A prophet named Malachi (Mal 1:1). Some ancient Jewish tradition (the Targum and the Talmud, Megillah 15a, in one opinion) identified him with Ezra, since 'Malachi' means 'my messenger'.
authorship.scholarly: Because *mal'akhi* means 'my messenger' and echoes Mal 3:1, many scholars think it is a title rather than a personal name, making the book anonymous; the heading 'the burden of the word of the LORD' matches Zech 9:1 and Zech 12:1, suggesting the three were once collected together. The content is generally dated to the mid 5th century BC, after the second temple was rebuilt and before or around the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah.

alternatives.label: Earlier, soon after the temple's completion

audience: The post-exilic community in Judah, especially priests offering blemished sacrifices and people grown cynical about God's love and justice.
setting: Jerusalem under Persian rule, with a functioning temple and a governor (Mal 1:8), but with lax worship, broken marriages and neglected tithes.
purpose: To answer the people's cynical questions, to rebuke careless priests and covenant-breaking, to call for wholehearted worship, and to promise the coming of the LORD's messenger and of Elijah before the great day of the LORD.
themes: God's covenant love questioned and affirmed
Honour due to God in worship
The messenger who prepares the way
The day of the LORD and the sun of righteousness
Remember the law of Moses; Elijah will come

outline.title: The messenger of the covenant and refining judgment
Return to me: robbing God in tithes
The book of remembrance and the coming day

bigStory: In Christian Bibles Malachi closes the Old Testament with a promise of the messenger and of Elijah, and the Gospels open by announcing that John the Baptist is that forerunner (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10-14; Luke 1:17). Its call to remember Moses and wait for Elijah ties Law and Prophets together, as they appear again with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3).
canonNote: Last of the Twelve and the last book of the Protestant Old Testament; the Hebrew Bible instead ends with Chronicles, and Hebrew Bibles number English Mal 4:1-6 as Mal 3:19-24. The Latin Vulgate and older Catholic Bibles such as the Douay-Rheims place the deuterocanonical *1 and 2 Maccabees* after Malachi, at the end of the Old Testament (modern Catholic Bibles such as the NAB place them after Esther). They recount the Jewish revolt against Antiochus IV Epiphanes (167–164 BC) and the rededication of the temple remembered at Hanukkah. Orthodox Bibles also include *3 Maccabees*, with *4 Maccabees* in an appendix; Protestant Bibles that print 1–2 Maccabees place them among the Apocrypha.
